title: TCC Database Manipulation via Launchctl and Unprotected SIP
shortTitle: TCC Database Manipulation via Launchctl and Unprotected SIP
summary: This detection strategy covers manipulation of the macOS consent database and the persistence that often follows it. That database records which applications may reach the camera, the microphone, the screen and user data, so editing it grants an application access that the user never approved. Direct writes to the consent store, use of the launch control utility to load an unsigned or user writable agent, and a report that system integrity protection is disabled give the pattern. The rule fails because legitimate administration tools also write consent entries and load agents, so the writing process, its signature and the protection status must be correlated.

beginner.definition: This detection looks at a list on a Mac. The list records which programs may use the camera, the microphone and your files. Attackers edit that list so their own program is allowed. They may also start their program through the Mac job scheduler. The alert fires when the list is changed outside a normal prompt. It also fires when the protection around the list is turned off.
beginner.whyItMatters: On a Mac, an application must ask you before it can use the camera, the microphone or your contacts. Your answer is stored in a database called the transparency consent and control database. If an attacker can write to that database directly, no prompt appears and the application quietly gains access. You are never asked, so you cannot refuse. Watching the database and the job scheduler together shows access that was never granted.
howItWorks: The endpoint security agent records a write to the consent database file, together with the writing process and the user.
Process telemetry records the launch control utility when it loads or starts a job definition from a user writable path.
The rule also checks whether system integrity protection is enabled, because that protection normally blocks writes to the consent store.
Each match is enriched with the signing status of the writing process and of its parent.
The alert fires when an unsigned or unusual process writes the consent store. It also fires when a job loads from a temporary folder.
Analysts then check the consent daemon log for a user prompt that would explain the write.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital sign-in sheet, but this one lists who may enter the medicine room. A clerk who can edit the sheet adds a name without asking the manager. The new person then walks in with a valid looking entry. Nobody was ever asked. The detection watches the sheet and the pen, not the person walking through the door.
takeaways: The consent database is the record of what the user allowed, so direct writes bypass the user entirely.
System integrity protection normally blocks those writes, so a disabled status matters as much as the write.
Look for a matching user prompt in the consent daemon log to tell legitimate writes from forced ones.

objectives: Describe what the macOS consent database records and why applications must not write to it directly
Identify the telemetry that shows a write to the consent store and the process responsible
Explain how the launch control utility is used to start a job definition and why the source path matters
Explain the role of system integrity protection in preventing consent store changes
Correlate a consent write with the absence of a user prompt in the platform log
Build an allow list for management agents that legitimately write consent entries
dataSources: macOS endpoint security framework telemetry for file writes to the user consent database, with the responsible process
macOS unified log entries from the consent daemon showing decisions, prompts and denied requests
Process execution records for the launch control utility including full arguments and job definition path
System integrity protection status reported by the platform configuration utility at boot and on demand
Code signing and notarisation status of any process that wrote the consent store or loaded the job
logic: The pattern is a write to the macOS consent database, or the loading of a job definition, by a process that is not the platform consent service or an approved management agent. Correlate the file write record with the signing identity of the responsible process, the path of the launch agent definition, and the integrity protection status, then check the consent daemon log for a user prompt in the preceding minute. The benign case is a mobile device management agent applying an approved profile, or an application writing its own entry immediately after the user answered a prompt. The malicious case pairs an unsigned writer with a job definition in a download or temporary folder on a host where protection is disabled.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Consent Store Write Or Unsigned Launch Agent Loaded
# logsource:
#   product: macos
detection:
  selection_consent:
    EventType: 'file_write'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '/Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db'
  selection_launch:
    EventType: 'exec'
    Image|endswith: '/bin/launchctl'
    CommandLine|contains: 'load'
  filter_mdm:
    SigningID|startswith: 'com.apple'
  condition: (selection_consent or selection_launch) and not filter_mdm
level: high
falsePositives: Mobile device management agents that write consent entries as part of an approved configuration profile
Administrators running the platform configuration utility to review protection status after a support case
Applications that write their own consent record immediately after the user answered the prompt
Developer tools that load a launch agent from a build directory during local testing
tuningNotes: Allow the mobile device management agent and the platform consent service by signing identity, then baseline which third party applications write the consent store in your fleet. Scope the job loading condition to downloads, temporary directories and user home folders, and drop the bare command name. Correlate each write with the absence of a matching user prompt within the previous minute, which removes legitimate application consent writes. Filtering on those folders loses coverage of an attacker who installs a job under the system library folder, so keep a separate lower severity rule for job definitions written into system paths.
